title: Influence Is a Practice, Not a Personality
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that influence is a learnable set of habits rather than a trait, and she builds the case by re-reading Dale Carnegie's How to Win Friends & Influence People. She distils four practices she uses with clients: lead with curiosity instead of criticism, recognise effort often, speak to the other person's incentives, and let others co-author the solution. Each practice comes with a try-today action, a level-up step and a hybrid-work example, which makes the piece easy to apply. Her move is to treat Carnegie's 1936 advice as still sound because the human levers of trust and persuasion have not changed with Slack, AI and dashboards. She concedes that Carnegie can read as manipulative if followed blindly, and she frames the lessons as respect, attention and empathy rather than technique. The result is a practical leadership-communication primer anchored in a classic text.
points: Replacing a piece of criticism with a curious question, such as asking what obstacles someone ran into, surfaces the real story and keeps people from getting defensive.
Frequent, specific recognition (a one-line Friday note, praise that names the actual contribution) builds loyalty and spreads as a team norm.
Persuasion works when change is framed around what the listener already wants; the same restructuring read as job cuts or as better customer service depending on framing.
People commit to solutions they helped create, so a leader should resist proposing first and let the group shape the answer.
Carnegie's advice endures and should be applied with judgment, because uncritical use can slide into people-pleasing.
quotes: Carnegie argued that direct criticism almost never works. It triggers defensiveness rather than change. Even if people nod along, the message rarely lands - in many cases, simply because they are upset.
Too often, recognition gets rationed out as if it were a scarce resource. Yet, it costs nothing to notice when someone has gone the extra mile.
Recognition is also contagious. A team that sees its leader acknowledge effort starts acknowledging each other. It builds a culture where appreciation is normal, not exceptional.

Leaders often announce new initiatives in terms of their own priorities, like efficiency and growth. But people follow when they see how the change helps them: less frustration, more autonomy, better outcomes for clients.

This is serious strategy, not a cheap trick. Studies in organisational behaviour show that involvement drives buy-in far more than instruction ever could. Whether you’re running a workshop or managing a project, the smartest move might be to speak less and ask more.
In the end, influence is all about respect, attention and empathy - currencies that never depreciate. For leaders in any industry, these currencies matter more than ever.
